claims.text: Rapid quenching of nominal FeCoNiTi produces a dual-phase microstructure containing an fcc solid solution and hexagonal C14 Laves precipitates.
The FeCoNiTi system exhibits ferromagnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
Coexistence with the C14 Laves phase enhances the coercivity of the FeCoNiTi alloy to approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
The C14 phase has a Ti-rich sublattice, while the adjacent fcc matrix is Fe/Co-rich.
Strong antiferromagnetic coupling is established between the Ti-rich C14 sublattice and the Fe/Co-rich fcc matrix.
Antiferromagnetic coupling suppresses the effective magnetic moment and net saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
C14–fcc phase boundaries create high-energy domain-wall pinning sites.
Changing Ti content and cooling rate controls the C14 volume fraction and C14–fcc interfacial area.
Annealing can stabilize the phase distribution without coarsening the C14 precipitates.
Thermal activation at 400 K would otherwise reduce coercivity.
The fcc–C14 interface is coherent or semi-coherent.
Electronic hybridization at the fcc–C14 interface mediates antiferromagnetic exchange.
Ti atoms in the C14 phase possess magnetic moments that couple antiferromagnetically to Fe and Co moments in the neighboring fcc phase.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling creates a local magnetic-anisotropy barrier.
The combined anisotropy and domain-wall-pinning energy landscape increases the field required for magnetization reversal.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments and a lack of strong pinning mechanisms.
The dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy will have lower saturation magnetization than a Ti-free fcc Fe-Co-Ni equivalent.
Coercivity enhancement requires a C14 stoichiometry and crystallographic orientation that maximize interfacial contact.
The coercivity enhancement will disappear if the C14 phase becomes nonmagnetic or magnetically decoupled through excessive Ti segregation or amorphization.
Spin-polarized GGA-PBE density-of-states calculations can test the proposed magnetic electronic structure at the Fermi level.
